title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win statewide in Texas since 1994
full_text:
By Nolan D. McCaskill
Nov 3 (Reuters) - State Representative James Talarico won the US Senate race in Texas on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating President Donald Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton to end Democrats’ 32-year statewide losing streak and give his party a major boost in the battle for Senate control.
It was a striking Democratic breakthrough in a state Republicans have long dominated. Trump carried the state by 14 percentage points in 2024. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, has been at the center of controversies that include a 2023 impeachment and a securities fraud case.
Talarico, a four-term state legislator and one of the nation’s top Senate fundraisers, overcame heavy outside spending in the most expensive Senate race of the cycle. He began as an underdog against former US Representative Colin Allred, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee, who later withdrew to run for Congress again.
Talarico went on to defeat US Representative Jasmine Crockett for the Democratic nomination, dealing a political blow to his former state legislative colleague.
Republicans spent more than $316 million to retain the seat. Republican US Senator John Cornyn was ousted in a primary runoff after Trump endorsed Paxton. Republican leaders had viewed Cornyn as the stronger general-election candidate.
Paxton used his role as attorney general to sue former President Joe Biden’s administration more than 100 times.
Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday’s elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

title: Top takeaways from the US midterm elections
full_text:
By Tim Reid and Trevor Hunnicutt
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Americans went to the polls on Tuesday in midterm elections that will determine who controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
Here are some takeaways from the elections.
A BLUE WAVE
Opinion polls ahead of the midterms showed a significant chance of a strong Democratic night, with the party favored to reclaim the US House and competing for control of the Senate.
But the scale of the Democratic gains suggested something larger: a potential blue wave that was extending well beyond the traditional battlegrounds and deep into Republican territory.
In Texas, James Talarico routed Republican Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat senator-elect in 38 years. Democrats have been dreaming of turning the Lone Star blue for decades.
In flipping the Senate seat in South Carolina, the party also made history. Democrats have not won a US Senate race in South Carolina this century, and the win by Annie Andrews over Republican Senator Darline Graham became another defining upset of the night.
In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown prevailed, while in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton easily defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. Democrats last won a Senate seat in Kansas in 1932, during the Great Depression.
Democrats were projected by US media outlets to win back control of both the US House and the Senate.
Winning back Congress could be a double-edged sword for Democrats, however.
Voters likely will look to Democrats to address their economic concerns and not just oppose Trump. But they will be limited in what legislation they can pass as the president retains veto power. Trump could also say Democrats are now at the very least equally culpable for the state of the economy.
Trump told The New York Times he would accept the election results and was prepared to work with Democrats.
AN ANGRY ELECTORATE
Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans paid the price on Tuesday.
Early results and exit polls showed an electorate in a sour mood, delivering a strong rebuke of Trump and his agenda as voters expressed deep unhappiness about high prices and the direction of the country.
Many said they feel worse off than two years ago and nearly 9 in 10 identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets that included major television networks and the Associated Press.
Trump was elected in 2024 on a promise to arrest high inflation, but his tariffs on foreign goods and war against Iran have only worsened the economic situation for many Americans. His response on the campaign trail was to tell Americans to absorb the higher costs even as his popularity sank to record lows.
Nearly two-thirds of voters in the exit polls blamed Trump for high prices, while three-quarters said they were either angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country. Voters also expressed widespread concern over government corruption.
Democratic victories on Tuesday suggested Trump’s 19-state campaign blitz for Republican candidates in recent weeks had done little to improve his standing with voters.
REJECTING TRUMP’S PICKS
It wasn’t just a bad night for Republicans; it was a bad night for Trump’s judgment. He suffered a series of personal defeats as several candidates he had elevated over the objections of local Republicans struggled in races the party had expected to win.
Trump’s handpicked Senate candidates in South Carolina and North Carolina, Graham and Michael Whatley, lost their races, while Paxton in Texas was soundly beaten. Trump’s choices left Republicans fighting on the defensive in states where they had been favored to win.
The losses are likely to revive questions about Trump’s political instincts, particularly his tendency to prioritize personal loyalty over candidates with broader electoral appeal.
The exit polls showed that the coalition of voters that powered his 2024 victory is badly fractured. Republicans recorded sharp declines in support among Black men, Latinos and young voters.
ECONOMY TRUMPS FEAR
In the closing weeks of the campaign, and lacking a coherent economic message, Trump and his fellow Republicans tried to paint Democrats as dangerous radicals and communists who would destroy the country if elected.
The scare tactics didn’t work. Voters were far more focused on the price of groceries and gas and wanted to hear more from Trump about how he would lower costs.
During the summer, Trump repeatedly argued that if Democrats won, "it’s going to be a communist country." He said Democratic establishments in various states had been replaced by "crazed lunatics and radicals."
Fear has often worked as a tactic in US elections, but in the end, Trump could not persuade voters that Democrats, one of the country’s two main political parties, really posed an existential threat to the United States.

title: Palantir shares retreat despite U.S. commercial sales spike
full_text:
Investing.com - Palantir shares slumped by more than 5% at the open of U.S. trading on Tuesday, dragged down by a soft indicator of future revenue that overshadowed otherwise solid third-quarter results.
The artificial intelligence-focused data analytics group logged earnings per share of $0.44, driven by a 96% surge in sales to $2.31 billion that was powered by robust commercial and government contracts in the United States. The two numbers -- along with a fourth-quarter outlook for sales of $2.649 billion-$2.653 billion and operating income of $1.64 billion-$1.644 billion -- outpaced estimates. Free cash flow also ticked up to $1.196 billion.
For the full year, the company raised its revenue forecast to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, implying annual growth of approximately 91%. It also increased its U.S. commercial revenue growth forecast to at least 143%, with revenue expected to exceed $3.56 billion.
U.S. commercial revenue climbed 148% versus a year ago to $984 million, up 29% from the previous quarter and exceeding U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time in the company’s history. Government revenue rose 96% year-over-year. Companies have been accelerating investments in AI as they race to integrate the technology into operational workflows.
Chief Executive Alex Karp said the growing adoption of what he called sovereign AI was creating a widening divide between institutions capable of deploying the technology and those falling behind.
Still, analysts flagged that growth in total contract value -- a tracker of the total dollar amount of all contracts signed during the quarter that helps shed light on possible incoming sales -- slowed to 6% versus a year ago. In the second quarter, the figure stood at 49%.
"[T]he headline income/cash flow statement figures are great (healthy beat-and-raise on revenue/operating income with very strong cash flow) but in the glass-half-empty mindset that tech finds itself in, people may walk away fairly neutral (or even modestly underwhelmed given some of the TCV details)," analysts at Vital Knowledge said in a note.
AI-exposed stocks have gyrated in recent weeks, driven by worries around the sustainability of large debt- and equity-fueled spending a rapid build-out of critical AI infrastructure like data centers and chips.

title: Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia race, becomes first Black woman elected governor of US state
full_text:
By Kat Stafford
Nov 3 - Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won Georgia’s race for governor on Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US state and delivering Democrats a victory in one of the nation’s most closely divided political battlegrounds.
The former Atlanta mayor, who will also be the first female governor of the state, defeated Republican businessman Rick Jackson, according to US media projections.
She succeeds Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who is leaving office after serving two consecutive terms. Bottoms, 56, also previously served as a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement.
The victory marked a new milestone for Black women in American politics, who have long been a core base within the Democratic Party but remain underrepresented in the nation’s highest elected offices. The same evening, Stacey Plaskett was elected governor of the US Virgin Islands, a US territory, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US jurisdiction.
In Florida, Republican US Representative Byron Donalds was elected governor. Donalds is the first Black Republican to be elected governor in the US.
Bottoms’ win also marks a significant shift in Georgia state politics, where Black voters have formed a central part of the Democratic coalition that helped to turn the reliably Republican state into a national battleground.
Republicans had controlled the governor’s office for more than two decades.
Jackson, the billionaire founder of healthcare staffing company Jackson Healthcare, cast himself as a political outsider and campaigned on tax cuts, public safety and reducing government regulation.
Bottoms’ victory comes eight years after fellow Democrat Stacey Abrams became the first Black woman nominated for governor by a major US political party.
Abrams lost governor’s races in Georgia in 2018 and 2022, but her campaigns helped to build a multigenerational, multiracial coalition that boosted Democratic turnout, helped elect two Democratic US senators and delivered Georgia’s electoral votes to a Democratic presidential candidate for the first time in decades.

title: BMW cuts 2026 auto margin outlook to break-even; keeps cash flow target

Investing.com -- BMW (ETR:BMWG) on Wednesday cut its 2026 profit forecast for its car business to break-even but kept its cash flow target, even as weak China sales and tariffs weigh.

Forecast return on capital employed, which measures profit against money tied up in the business, fell to between -1% and 1% from 1% to 5%.

Pretax profit included a financial result of €494 million versus €68 million a year earlier, driven primarily by positive valuation effects from interest rate hedging transactions.

A settlement in the legal dispute over the Integrated Braking System also lowered cost of sales.

Rogers also devoted significant effort to courting Jewish voters who may have been uneasy with El-Sayed’s opposition to US military aid for Israel and his characterization of Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide.
But Rogers struggled to overcome voter concerns about the economy and Trump’s low ratings. In the closing weeks of the race, he broke with the president on the war in Iran and the US trade dispute with Canada, arguing that ending both was necessary to help bring down costs for businesses and consumers.

title: ’A mandate for change’: Democrats remake Texas politics in election rout
full_text:
By Brad Brooks
Nov 4 (Reuters) - Texas Democrats, shut out of every statewide office for more than three decades, have toppled Republicans from the top of the ballot to the bottom, remaking the political landscape of the nation’s largest conservative state in a single earth-shattering night.
While James Talarico’s victory in the US Senate race and Gina Hinojosa’s defeat of three-term Governor Greg Abbott stole the headlines, Democratic candidates also triumphed in a series of lower-profile races on Tuesday, giving them the power to reshape the state’s economic and political future.
The Democratic wins were fueled by record turnout -- especially in Latino communities that have borne the brunt of President Donald Trump’s immigration sweeps -- and cracks in the Republican coalition, as some conservatives and independents soured on inflation and the war with Iran.
“I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state,” Hinojosa said in her victory speech. “The voters have delivered a mandate for change and it is change they will get.”
Talarico, in a nod to the hundreds of millions of dollars that Elon Musk poured into his opponent’s campaign, told his supporters “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”
Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, who as head of the state Senate has driven Texas’ hard-right legislative agenda for more than a decade, lost to Vikki Goodwin, a state representative little known outside of the capital Austin.
Democrat Nathan Johnson captured the attorney general’s office -- which Republicans have used for decades to challenge the policies of Democratic presidents in court.
Democrats also won races for comptroller, land commissioner, agriculture commissioner and railroad commissioner -- key offices that oversee the state budget, its public lands, its farm economy and its oil and gas industry.
As was true elsewhere in the US, efforts by Texas Republicans to redraw congressional maps to their advantage largely backfired on Tuesday. Tejano singer Bobby Pulido ousted Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz in the Rio Grande Valley; Democrat Katy Padilla Stout won the sprawling 23rd district.
A ’WAKE-UP CALL’
The last open question on Wednesday was whether Democrats would also take the Texas House, which Republicans have controlled since 2003.
Erika Kinder, a Republican voter attending the watch party for losing Senate candidate Ken Paxton, said she hoped the losses would re-energize her party.
“The Texas GOP has been a little softer and unenthusiastic and this is probably a good wake-up call,” she said. “I think we’ll be right as rain in two to four years.”
Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democrats, predicted in a September interview with Reuters that the party would win at the top of the ticket -- and “we’re going to surprise you down ballot, too.”
Scudder emerged from the party’s grassroots and tried to steer it back to its populist roots. Talarico, Hinojosa and others on the Democratic ticket focused intensely on pocketbook issues and government corruption, even as their Republican opponents tried to center transgender rights and other culture war issues.
“This has been two years of everyone in this state trying to build in regions that have been ignored for a very long time, and in communities that have been taken for granted,” Scudder said weeks before the election. “It’s going to culminate in wins.”

title: Democratic sweep adds new twist to markets’ Iran, AI, and debt worries

By Dhara Ranasinghe and Ankur Banerjee
LONDON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - A sweeping Democratic win in US midterm elections is the latest curve ball to markets grappling with the repercussions of the Iran war and an AI boom that has bolstered growth and inflation, just as the world’s biggest economy’s debt load mounts.
While the overall market reaction to the results was modest on Wednesday, with equities higher in Europe, investors are bracing for volatility to continue. Attention fell on two areas in particular: the direction of an Iran war that has helped drive oil prices up 70% this year and a contentious debate over US fiscal spending.
"The biggest potential market implications could be if, with the midterms now out of the way, the President (Donald Trump) decides to escalate in the Middle East," said Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, which manages almost $600 billion of assets.
"If escalation... were to follow and energy prices then move higher it could hurt both stocks and bonds at the same time."
As the Iran war persists, oil prices have remained stuck above $100 a barrel, pushing up fuel costs for consumers and businesses. Central banks, meanwhile, are alert to the risks of a spillover into a broader price surge that necessitates much higher interest rates.
The Federal Reserve has missed its inflation target for more than half a decade. Euro zone inflation rose to a three-year high at 4% in October on expensive energy and was set to rise further in the coming months, data on Wednesday showed, reaffirming market bets for a December European Central Bank rate hike.
Geopolitical risks remained high since Trump retains control of foreign policy, analysts said.
In addition to the Iran war, the US capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and Trump’s tariff threats to European allies over Greenland earlier this year also caught investors off guard.
"We probably have to brace ourselves for significant foreign policy noise in the two final years of the Trump presidency," said Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding.
FROM AI BUILD OUT TO DEBT
Fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny following the Democrat win was an immediate focus for the market.
Opinion polls have shown Democratic voters favoring more control over AI, and investors expect the Democratic-controlled Congress to apply more scrutiny to the sector.
Still, world stocks overcame initial wobbles and were higher, while US stock futures, rose, having fallen by as much as 2% overnight.
"AI is such a core part of the US growth story. So whoever is in government will try and get the best of both worlds - support the build out while respecting affordability concerns," said Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, nothing that the S&P stock index has been higher a year after midterms on each occasion since the end of World War Two.
And Wednesday’s market reaction was broadly in line with that logged a day after the last midterm elections in 2022. At that time, the S&P closed 1.4% higher a day after the vote, while Europe’s STOXX index rallied 1.8%, the euro jumped over 2% and gold gained 3.1%.
Still, investors have been getting nervous about market resiliency. AI’s capital-investment surge and highly indebted governments have helped drive up borrowing costs to multidecade highs, exposing markets faultlines.
Shah added that she would be watching what happens to fiscal policy, which could be even more constrained following the election result.
Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with analysts expressing relief that Trump’s promise to hand out $5,000 checks to US adults in the event of a Republican victory would not materialise.
Democratic control of Congress is likely to mean stronger oversight of fiscal policies and restraint around what Trump could do in terms of increased spending, said Societe Generale’s global head of emerging markets research Phoenix Kalen.
"That places more tighter limits on fiscal policy and should help to ease pressure a bit on US bond yields," she said.
Concern about a US debt pile that recently topped $40 trillion has helped push up government bond yields this year.
Congress has postponed a contentious debate over fiscal 2027 spending until after the midterms, setting up a December 11 deadline to reach a funding agreement.
The deadline for raising the debt ceiling is unlikely to be arrive until late 2027, Democrats could use the so-called X-date as leverage in negotiations with Republicans over spending and tax policy, pressing for concessions in exchange for votes to address the borrowing limit.
"We expect market volatility to continue," said Shah. "It will be white-knuckled ride for the next year."

The gains followed landslide midterm victories for Democrats who oppose data centers, including in Texas, likely accelerating a backlash against the power-hungry, water-intensive and noisy facilities that are at the heart of the AI boom but increasingly unpopular with local communities.
"Conceptually, post-election, there may be a bit of a slowdown or some bumps in the road for future data-center build-out," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth.
"The hyperscalers (large tech companies) already have data centers, so those assets are more valuable now because there’s not going to be an overbuild of data centers. The tech giants have been building capacity at a blistering pace, with plans to spend more than $740 billion this year, up from roughly $400 billion last year. That far outstrips smaller AI cloud rivals such as CoreWeave and Nebius.
Shares of smaller players including Applied Digital and Iren plunged between 6% and 13% on fears that curbs on data-center construction could derail their debt-fueled expansion plans. The companies have been spending several times their revenue to meet a swelling backlog of orders.
"The biggest worry of the night for tech investors and the AI trade was around the state of Texas, where ~25%-30% of data-center gigawatts and capacity will come from," said Dan Ives, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives.

title: Crypto’s midterm spending spree stumbles as Democrats rack up big wins
full_text:
By Hannah Lang and Michelle Price
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The crypto industry’s roughly $200 million spending spree this election stumbled Tuesday, as some of its most expensive and high-profile targets, including the Senate race in Ohio, did not go its way.
While the industry won most of the races it targeted, those losses raised questions among lobbyists about whether it had backed the right candidates.
The greatest blow for the industry came in Ohio, where Democrat and crypto skeptic Sherrod Brown decisively won his race to return to the Senate, despite crypto political action committees spending more than $60 million to defeat him.
The race was one of the most expensive in the Senate’s history. Strategists viewed it as a major test of crypto’s political clout after the Senate in September voted against advancing major crypto legislation known as the Clarity Act due to opposition from Democrats, in a blow for an industry that has grown close to President Donald Trump.
Some progressive Democratic primary candidates also successfully attacked opponents over their crypto ties.
"We see this as souring the political environment for crypto," said Jaret Seiberg, an analyst with TD Cowen, in a note on Tuesday.
The leading industry super PAC, Fairshake, notched one high-profile victory, as it and its affiliates spent at least $13.5 million to defeat Nebraska independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn, a former labor union leader. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who voted for the Clarity Act.
“As the biggest spender in the Nebraska Senate race, we’re proud to have helped Sen. Ricketts weather the waves of a hard-fought cycle," said Geoff Vetter, a spokesperson for Fairshake.
Fairshake, whose chief backers include Coinbase, Ripple and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, threw its financial heft behind 32 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats — whom it considered supporters of the industry’s priorities.
So far, it has won 29 of the 34 races it spent on, with several races not yet called. Of the six House candidates on whom Fairshake spent $1 million or more, so far it has won three.
"Newly elected and current members will have a choice: protect consumers and American jobs or fight progress," Fairshake’s Vetter said.
The crypto industry has spent roughly half a billion dollars over the past two election cycles to build a bipartisan coalition of congressional allies to advance its interests.
In 2024, it helped elect dozens of crypto-friendly lawmakers who later came together to pass a law to help promote adoption of dollar-backed tokens known as stablecoins.
The Clarity Act’s defeat was a major setback, and with Democrats taking Congress, the industry now faces oversight and potential investigations, particularly its ties to Trump.
Cryptocurrencies posted overnight losses on the results, but recovered on Wednesday. Bitcoin, the world’s largest cryptocurrency, was last up 3.1% above $80,000.
Crypto executives frequently say the long-term trend is still favorable.
"Where crypto is today compared to we were two years ago is night and day," said Stu Alderoty, chief legal officer at Ripple, speaking before the results. However, on the possibility of Democratic probes into Trump’s crypto business dealings, he said: "I think the writing is on the wall.”

title: Blue wave crashes through US state government races
full_text:
By Julia Harte
Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrats’ takeover of the US Congress on Tuesday was replicated at the state level, with the party flipping Republican-held governors’ offices in at least five states and poised to seize full control of state government in at least six more.
Democratic victories mean the party, for the first time in years, will control a majority of the governorships, including traditional conservative strongholds such as Texas, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated well-financed Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the first Latina governor in the state’s history.
The wins extended beyond governors’ mansions. Democratic candidates seized control of both state legislative chambers in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, giving the party "trifecta" control of the legislature and governor’s office in those states. They also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.
On top of giving Democrats more control over state laws on minimum wage, data centers, abortion access, and other hot-button issues, the wins could affect future national elections by changing how US congressional districts are drawn, how elections are administered, and how results are certified, according to policy experts.
Some of the biggest and most surprising wins came in battleground states that have been key to President Donald Trump’s election victories, and where Republican-led legislatures in recent years redrew congressional district boundaries to favor their party.
In at least three states — Georgia, Indiana and Ohio — Democrats also ousted incumbent Republican secretaries of state: the office that typically oversees election administration and certification of results.
All those outcomes are "very significant" for future US elections, according to Michael Berkman, a political science professor and director of Penn State University’s McCourtney Institute for Democracy.
He said Republicans won a similar sweep of state-level offices during former President Barack Obama’s first midterm election in 2010, which allowed them to pass election laws, redraw congressional districts, and give their party more control over how elections were administered in some states.
"So this gives Democrats an opportunity to really start to claw that back," Berkman said.
The new Democratic leaders and legislators will likely try to undo some conservative policies that have recently dominated the national discourse, such as abortion restrictions and data center incentives, experts said.
But the incoming Democrats will also take office with "a huge backlog of liberal legislation that they want to do," said Chris Warshaw, a professor at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy.
Their top priorities will likely address voters’ concerns about affordability, such as raising the minimum wage, expanding the federal Medicaid health insurance program and protecting labor rights, Warshaw said.
In Texas and Georgia, Republicans looked likely to lose control of the state legislatures for the first time in more than 20 years, yielding control over one chamber in each state to Democrats.
"The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get," Hinojosa said in a victory speech on Tuesday night.
Texas and Georgia voters also elected Democratic attorneys general for the first time in more than a decade, replacing Republican incumbents who had frequently sued past Democratic presidents over federal policies with which they disagreed.
As a result, "those places will stop being fountains for initial lawsuits, and start being fountains for lawsuits that are challenging things that Trump is doing," said Jim Battista, associate professor of political science at the University at Buffalo, State University of New York.

title: Dollar slips to over one-month low on U.S. midterm results, mixed economic data
full_text:
Investing.com -- The U.S. dollar fell to its lowest level in over a month on Wednesday, as currency market participants digested a Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterm elections and weighed potential policy ramifications that could possibly dent economic growth.
Watchers of monetary policy also received some mixed economic data ahead of Friday’s all-important U.S. nonfarm payrolls report.
At 14:21 ET (19:21 GMT), the U.S. dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of six major peers, fell 0.3% to 101.55. The gauge earlier hit a session low at 101.10, its lowest since September 30.
Democrats seize control of both chambers of Congress
Figures from the Associated Press showed the Democrats securing a majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, even with some votes still yet to be counted.
In the 100-seat Senate, Democrats have won 54 seats, with two races still to be called, according to AP projections. Democrats have also seized 228 seats in the House of Representatives, surpassing the 218-seat threshold needed to have a majority in the lower chamber.
Notable Democratic victories included James Talarico taking winning in a Senate race in the traditional Republican stronghold of Texas, along with Abdul El-Sayed emerging victorious in a Senate race in the key swing state of Michigan. The Democrats flipped at least seven seats from the Republicans in the Senate.
The outcome represents a sharp repudiation of the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, a time during which Republicans held slim majorities in the House and Senate. At least some Democratic approval will now be required for legislation to pass through Congress from January, although Trump will retain his ability to veto bills without the threat of a Congressional override.
The immediate consequences of the results could be stricter regulation at the federal and local level of artificial intelligence-related investments such as the construction of data centers. Given that AI infrastructure buildouts have boosted the U.S. economy, any hit to it could affect growth and take the shine off the world’s premier currency.
"The most important policy implication of a Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterm election is a prospective slowdown of data center construction. And insofar as the AI-driven infrastructure investment cycle has supported growth in the U.S., especially, any politically-driven slowdown would be adverse for the USD. This is among the three most important factors driving the value of the USD in FX markets in the medium term, along with oil/war and European debt sustainability," Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie, said.
"When looking for FX ideas following the mid-term election, consider the CAD. Canada is the U.S.’s largest trade partner, so would benefit more than others if we get a ’softer’ Trump. Reciprocally, lowered U.S. tariffs on Canada would help directly address the ’cost of living’ issue that hurt Republican candidates. And rapprochement would help build the strong hemispheric alliance that may help Trump rebuild his legacy project in the last half of his term. We still like selling AUD/CAD," he added.
The Canadian dollar had indeed strengthened to $1.3975 on Wednesday.
Away from the midterms, the U.S. economic calendar was in focus. ADP’s monthly private employment report showed the addition of 86k jobs in October, comfortably higher than expectations of 67k and matching September’s figure. The data indicated a solid labor market, coming a day after U.S. job openings hit a four-month high. All eyes are now on Friday’s nonfarm payrolls report.
Elsewhere, the Institute for Supply Management said economic activity in the U.S. services sector cooled slightly in October from September, but remained in expansion territory. A separate report from S&P Global showed a similar trend.
Euro set for best day since mid-October
Across the Atlantic, the euro capitalized on the greenback’s retreat, jumping 0.3% to $1.1220 and heading for its best session since October 15.
The sharp advance occurred despite underlying domestic macroeconomic data highlighting persistent growth drag across the single-currency bloc. The S&P Global Eurozone Composite PMI fell to 51.7 in October from 53.1 in September, hitting a four-month low and undershooting the preliminary estimate of 51.9.
The survey revealed that underlying economic expansion slowed sharply, with aggregate demand coming close to stalling, business confidence sinking to a five-month low, and rising input costs squeezing corporate profit margins.
Sterling climbs ahead of Bank of England decision
The sterling also advanced against the dollar, rising 0.4% to $1.3467, its highest in nearly two months.
Sterling drew support from the dollar unwind, but dealing desks refrained from chasing aggressive upside ahead of Thursday’s Bank of England (BOE) policy announcement.
With UK headline and services inflation proving stubborn, money markets are heavily positioning for the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to raise the key policy rate by 25 basis points to 4%.
"It’s likely that the BOE responds to trends in the UK data and the new UK Budget proposal with a ’hawkish hike’ in the Bank Rate at tomorrow’s MPC meeting," Macquarie’s Wizman said.
"Partly in anticipation of this tonal shift, EUR/ GBP has already slid much lower in the past five weeks and is probably not worth chasing downward. Still, the foundation for a stronger EUR/ GBP is not being put in place yet. That would happen, perhaps, with a resumption of stronger EU growth, clarity on EU debt sustainability, or peace in Russia-Ukraine," he added.
Roushni Nair and Pranav Kashyap contributed to this article

title: BOJ debated need for more rate hikes, scope for faster move, September minutes show
full_text:
By Leika Kihara
TOKYO, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Bank of Japan policymakers saw the need to keep raising interest rates, with one signalling the chance of faster-paced increases, minutes of the central bank’s September meeting showed on Thursday.
"If signs of an upward deviation in prices were observed, the BOJ would need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes," one member was quoted as saying in the minutes.
Another member said while the BOJ did not need to take hasty action, it should guide policy appropriately "to prevent excessive and persistent price rises," the minutes showed.
At its September meeting, the BOJ raised its key interest rate to a 31-year high of 1.25% and signalled a shift in its policy approach to one focused on keeping the rate of inflation from overshooting the bank’s 2% target.
The central bank kept its key interest rate steady at a subsequent meeting in October but signalled its vigilance to inflation risk, cementing market expectations for a hike in December.
At the September meeting, many board members projected consumer inflation to accelerate from autumn as surveys reflected an increasing number of price hikes for food items, the minutes showed.
Many members also shared the view that inflation risb will remain elevated due to a renewed rise in crude oil prices brought about by prolonged conflict in the Middle East, the minutes showed.
"The BOJ should continue to act in a timely manner without becoming overly cautious" about raising interest rates and seek to deepen analysis over inflation risk, one member was quoted as saying.

title: MercadoLibre falls on earnings miss, margin pressure

Investing.com -- MercadoLibre Inc (NASDAQ:MELI) reported third quarter results that missed earnings expectations, sending shares down 7.8% in after-hours trading Wednesday as investors reacted to the profit shortfall and declining operating margins.
The Latin American e-commerce and fintech company posted adjusted earnings per share of $8.83, missing the analyst consensus of $9.34 by $0.51. Revenue reached $10.75 billion, slightly above the $10.69 billion estimate and up 45% YoY. Income from operations totaled $676 million with a 6.3% margin, down from 7.0% in the prior quarter and representing a 6% decline YoY.
The margin compression reflected higher costs from expanded free shipping, new fulfillment capacity added ahead of peak season, and increased affiliate marketing spend in Brazil. Net shipping margin fell approximately 200 basis points as a percentage of gross merchandise volume since the first quarter of 2025, as the company absorbed costs from lower-priced items and more frequent shipments following its decision to lower free shipping thresholds.
"Mercado Libre delivered another quarter of strong growth in Q3’26, with net revenue and financial income of $10,750 million, up 45% YoY," the company stated, noting it gained market share in its three largest markets of Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina.
GMV grew 38% YoY to $23 billion, while total payment volume increased 53% to $109 billion. The company’s credit portfolio reached nearly $18 billion, up 62% YoY, with the credit card now representing 47% of the portfolio. Fintech monthly active users grew 29% to 93 million.
In Brazil, FX-neutral GMV grew 36% YoY with sold items up 45%. Mexico saw slower growth with FX-neutral GMV up 21% as tax reform and weaker consumption weighed on demand. Argentina posted 40% FX-neutral GMV growth despite soft consumption conditions.
The company expanded its fulfillment network by almost 20% quarter-over-quarter in square footage, contributing to near-term margin pressure. Sales and marketing expenses rose to 11.6% of net revenue from 11.2% in the prior quarter due to increased investment in Brazil’s affiliate program.
Net income was $448 million, up 6% YoY, with a 4.2% margin. The company completed a $1 billion investment grade bond issue in September.

title: Elon Musk’s business empire braces for Democratic wave as Texas flips blue
full_text:
By Aditya Soni
Nov 4 (Reuters) - As Republicans suffered a landslide defeat and Texas elected its first Democratic governor in more than three decades, one of the biggest losers of the US midterms was not on the ballot: billionaire Elon Musk.
The world’s richest man spent nearly half a billion dollars to back Republican candidates and keep Texas red - a state home to his automaker Tesla, rocket-to-AI company SpaceX and a planned chipmaking venture between the two.
Those bets unraveled as Democrats seized both chambers of Congress and Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in the Texas governor’s race, in a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump, a close Musk ally whom the billionaire helped elect.
Musk, who urged his followers on X to vote Republican as recently as Tuesday, now faces a resurgent Democratic Party that he has spent years antagonizing.
The GOP’s largest donor even threatened retaliation last month on his social media platform after a report said Democrats were considering probes into his companies if they won midterms.
Shares of SpaceX fell 5.5%, while Tesla was down 5.1% as both stocks lagged the broader market.
One of Musk’s biggest challenges could be slower approvals for the data centers crucial to tapping the $28.5 trillion addressable market that SpaceX touted to investors ahead of its IPO.
Analysts and experts expect Democrats to tighten scrutiny of data-center projects and push for construction moratoriums as local opposition grows over electricity costs.
"A Democratic sweep of Congress would put pressure on tech and potentially bring regulatory pressure on everything AI and possibly slow down the wild, wild west growth figures that we see daily and often take for granted," said Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management.
"Musk was the Hail Mary for Republicans leading down to the wire. Unfortunately, his large infusion of cash to back red states could not overcome higher utility bills, prices at the grocery store and prices at the gas pump."
Musk has also drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over restrictions on satellite communications used by Ukraine’s military, mass federal job cuts under his watch at DOGE and the government contracts and subsidies flowing to his companies.
One of the lawmakers is Robert Garcia, the next House Oversight Committee chair, who had a blunt two-word message for Republicans and their allies on Tuesday evening: "Lawyer up."
HINOJOSA PUSHES FOR DATA-CENTER MORATORIUM
In Texas, Musk will have to navigate an already strained relationship with Hinojosa. He will also face newly elected U.S. Senator James Talarico, against whom he spent heavily while backing Republican Ken Paxton.
Incoming governor Hinojosa had sued to obtain emails between Musk and Abbott and accused the former governor of selling out the Lone Star state by offering favorable deals to the billionaire.
She has also dismissed Abbott’s efforts to rein in data centers as political theater, calling instead for an immediate halt to new projects until lawmakers strengthened protections for local communities, as well as an end to tax breaks.
Musk himself appeared to make light of the hurdles. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," he posted on X, alluding to SpaceX’s ambitious plan to put data centers in orbit despite major challenges around cooling and repairs.
The company’s AI business is centered around Colossus and Colossus II, two of the world’s largest AI data centers near Memphis. Renting their computing power to customers including Anthropic has sent revenue soaring and helped SpaceX post its first profit as a public company.
But the company aims to nearly double capacity from 1.7 gigawatts at September-end to as much as 3 gigawatts by year-end, before scaling up to 13 gigawatts next year.
Any delays in bringing the capacity online may hamper Musk’s ambitious revenue targets and intensify scrutiny from investors growing wary about AI infrastructure’s mounting costs.
Chip research firm SemiAnalysis has identified more than 9 gigawatts of planned or developing capacity, including new facilities at SpaceX’s Starbase complex in Boca Chica, Texas.
That Boca Chica expansion could face resistance as Hinojosa has opposed the potential sale of a beachfront state park to SpaceX after Texas Monthly reported officials had discussed the deal.
"Let me be clear: Texas is not for sale," Hinojosa said last month. Musk, meanwhile, has deleted his election-day appeal to his followers to vote Republican.

title: Japan services activity expands for fifth month, PMI shows
full_text:
TOKYO, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Japan’s service sector expanded modestly in October as activity and new orders both rose slightly faster, a business survey showed on Thursday.
• The S&P Global final Japan Services Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) edged higher to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September, a survey by S&P Global showed, marking a fifth straight month of expansion but coming in below the flash reading of 52.0. The 50-mark separates growth from contraction
• New orders increased for a 28th straight month, with the pace of growth picking up from September, as firms cited firmer domestic demand, new clients and business development efforts as factors
• In contrast, foreign demand remained weak, though the decline in new export orders eased to its slowest since April
• Cost pressures eased further, with input price inflation decelerating for a fourth straight month to an eight-month low. Output price inflation also moderated, although charges have now risen every month for the past four and a half years
• Business confidence weakened to its lowest level since March, as concerns over inflation, an ageing population and labour shortages tempered optimism about growth in the defence and technology sectors, business expansion plans and increased tourism
• Persistent inflation "could also constrain demand and hiring in the months ahead," said Annabel Fiddes, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence
• "Whether growth loses further momentum and cost pressures ease will be important considerations for the Bank of Japan as it assesses further policy tightening," Fiddes added
• Employment rose only marginally, marking the weakest pace of job creation in the current 14-month hiring stretch, the survey showed. Companies cited expansion plans as factors for additions, while resignations and retirements limited overall headcount growth
• Japan’s composite output index slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, its softest growth pace since May. Stronger growth in services activity was countered by a slowdown in manufacturing output, sector data showed
